examples.name: Default decorative icon
examples.description: Decorative by default - hidden from assistive technology because a visible label already carries the meaning.

examples.name: Paired with a label
examples.description: The most common usage - an icon inside a control that already has a visible/accessible label.

examples.name: Informative, standalone icon
examples.description: The icon is the only content, so it needs its own accessible name.

examples.name: Small size
examples.description: The compact glyph size, e.g. inline with body-sm text.

examples.name: Spacious hit box
examples.description: A visually small icon centered in a larger click/touch target.

examples.name: Semantic color
examples.description: Color used because the icon itself carries that meaning (a success confirmation), not just for decoration.

examples.name: Inverse color on a dark surface

antiExamples.name: Icon alone with no accessible name
antiExamples.reason: If this is the only content in an interactive control (no visible text, no aria-label on the control), a screen reader announces nothing - use decorative={false} with a title, or add aria-label to the parent control.

antiExamples.name: Hardcoded fill color
antiExamples.reason: Icons must use the semantic color prop, not inline/hardcoded colors - use color="success" instead.

antiExamples.name: Icon used as a logo
antiExamples.reason: Icon is for functional glyphs, not brand identity - use the Logo primitive for brand marks/wordmarks.
